newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: C.EUROPE STATES SEE SECURITY AS TOP SUMMIT ISSUE.
newsitem.headline: C.EUROPE STATES SEE SECURITY AS TOP SUMMIT ISSUE.

text.p: Fifteen central European states began a summit in Austria on Friday and Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky said before the opening session the region's security and future ties with Russia were paramount.

"The Central European Initiative aims at bridging the differences between individual member countries and particularly on the question of security the CEI can make an important contribution," he told a news conference.
The CEI, including Italy and Austria, was formed in 1989 to discuss issues of security, politics and economics.
Vranitzky said the CEI had received a letter this week from Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin expressing Moscow's interest in a dialogue with the CEI.

In the letter, released by the group, Chernomyrdin said: "We consider the CEI to be an integral part of the all-European integration processes and an important component of the European architecture of the 21st century.
"I'm convinced that the establishment of relations between Russia and the CEI on the permanent basis...will benefit our countries."
Vranitzky said that, although Russia was not a member, it would be impossible for the CEI to ignore its influence over countries which once were members of the Soviet bloc.

"If we want to continue building the Europe of the 21st century then from my point of view the security construction has to be shaped in consultation and in dialogue with Russia," he said at the news conference held in the ornate congress hall of Austria's second largest city.
"There must be no security architecture without consultation with Russia," he added.

During the two-day summit, the CEI is due to admit Moldova as its 16th member. Vranitzky said there would probably be be a discussion on whether to approve former Yugoslavia as the 17th and final member.

The future of the former Yugoslav republics was one of the main agenda issues and Vranitzky said application of the U.S.-brokered Dayton peace accord and eventual reconstruction of former Yugoslavia were critical to the region.

"In my view the Dayton peace process still needs to be implemented on a number of fronts affecting the civilian area," Vranitzky said. "...Particularly in the civilian area the Dayton peace process is lagging behind."
He said the main components for peace were military security, reconstruction and repatriation of war refugees.

"If it does not work militarily there is no need to consider reconstruction and unless the people return to the country we cannot talk about human reconstruction," he said. "...This requires all our support."

Other issues on the agenda include the CEI's contribution to regional security and stability in cooperation with the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), the Council of Europe and the UN Economic Commission for Europe.
Vranitzky said the CEI's aim was to bring the countries of the region closer together and to improve cooperation in such areas as transport and energy.

"The CEI wants to be a platform for central and eastern Europe without wanting to be a rival to any of the existing organisations," said Rudolf Bogner, an Austrian foreign ministry official in charge of the summit's organisation.

The meeting will also examine relations between CEI member states and Baltic and Black Sea states, as well as with countries that have expressed interest in closer cooperation, including Russia, Turkey and Greece.
